title: Struct Layout, Alignment and Bit Fields
summary: How a struct sits in memory - alignment and padding, sizeof and offsetof, ordering fields to save space, _Alignof and _Alignas, flexible array members for variable-sized structs, bit fields for packed flags, and why binary files need explicit layouts.

cards.q: Why is `struct { char a; double b; char c; }` bigger than 10 bytes?
cards.a:
Padding keeps `b` and arrays of it aligned

`b` must start at a multiple of 8, and the size is rounded up to the struct's alignment: on a typical 64-bit system 1 + 7 padding + 8 + 1 + 7 = 24 bytes. Ordering the members largest first shrinks it to 16.

cards.q: Why are bit fields a poor choice for a file format?
cards.a:
Their layout is up to each compiler

The order and packing of the bits are implementation-defined, so another compiler may read them differently. Use shifts and masks on fixed-width integers.

cards.q: Where must a flexible array member go?
cards.a:
last in the struct

It has no fixed size, so nothing can come after it.
